title: Efficiënte ontwerpmethoden voor kostenefficiënte maskering: afwegingen bij zijkanaalbeveiliging in hardware
abstract: The main goal of the research is to contribute to countermeasures to protect hardware implementations of symmetric cryptographic algorithms against physical attacks. It can include both countermeasures against passive and active attacks. The research is aimed to study such concepts as masking, threshold implementations, randomness generation and many others in order to improve the security and performance of the hardware implementations against a more realistic adversary model. This contribution can help to define metrics for combined security and to develop procedures for their evaluation in the future.

title: Whole-slide images of tissue microarrays constructed from hepatocellular carcinoma patient specimens
abstract: This dataset contains whole-slide images (WSIs) of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue microarrays constructed from surgically resected hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patient specimens. The tissue microarrays include paired tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissues from a single-center HCC cohort, which were subjected to immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for ASF1B, MTHFD2, H3K27la and other markers. These high-resolution scanned images were used for subsequent quantitative analysis of protein expression levels and pathological evaluation in the associated study.

via TabPFN imputation, correlation filtering, and SEM.DDPM-based conditional synthetic patient generation over the 5D pathology latent space (healthy → maximal pathology).Downstream prediction title: With a Little Help From AI?! Governing Visual Hate Speech Through AI-Assisted Counter-Image Practices
abstract: The attention-grabbing and memorable nature of visuals makes them a powerful vehicle for spreading hate online. As platforms increasingly reconsider or scale back content moderation efforts, user-centered interventions are gaining importance as complementary governance strategies. While prior research demonstrates the effectiveness of empathy-based textual counter speech, little is known about the role of visual counter speech in mitigating hateful imagery. This preregistered study examines the effectiveness of user-centered interventions against visual hate speech. Using an experimental design (N = 666), we tested four interventions against a no-intervention control condition in response to hateful images targeting transgender persons: (a) empathy-based textual counter speech, (b) AI-generated generic counter images, (c) AI-generated specific counter images replicating elements of the original, and (d) platform-issued warning labels. Results show substantial variation across interventions. Empathy-based textual counter speech and AI-generated specific counter images showed the most consistent reductions in amplification-oriented behaviors, particularly forwarding. Visual interventions did not outperform textual counter speech, suggesting that effectiveness depends less on modality and more on the specificity and contextual alignment of the intervention. Furthermore, effectiveness varied with the intensity of the hate content. Interventions were most effective for humor-based, more ambiguously harmful content, whereas their impact diminished for more severe forms of hate. The consistent performance of AI-generated specific counter images further points to the potential of generative AI to provide users with a rapid, low-cost, and accessible means of producing context-sensitive counter speech.

title: Urdu Sukhan ASR: Accurate Urdu Speech Recognition at Half the Size of Whisper large-v3
abstract: We describe Urdu Sukhan ASR v1, an Urdu speech recognition model that also handles English and Urdu–English code-switching, and how it was trained and tested, including the rounds that failed. The model is a full fine-tune of Whisper large-v3-turbo on about 110 hours of transcribed audio per pass: public Urdu corpora, two audiobooks read by two narrators, with transcripts proofread by the author, Urdu–English clips we assembled, and no-speech audio. Against the base model with the same decoding, it makes fewer word errors on all seven held-out Urdu test sets, on average 39% fewer: from 30.9% to 12.7% on IndicVoices, from 39.8% to 28.1% on Common Voice speakers never seen in training and from 21.0% to 16.2% on FLEURS. On one- or two-word replies the error falls from 88.9% to 23.6%, on clips that switch from Urdu to English from 53.6% to 19.7%, and English stays at 4.9%. Two of the six training rounds learned to hear words in faint hiss; we trace this to training speech that was fainter than the hiss in our silence test, and we show that the single word Whisper models write on silence by default comes from a decoding rule that forbids an empty answer. With that rule off, our model writes nothing on 100 noise, music and silence clips and no speech score changes. We report speed on four machines in whisper.cpp, faster-whisper and Core ML, and a compression experiment whose 16-layer student was 1.9 times faster but not accurate enough to release. Loudness.ai technical report LA-RB-2026-004, version 1.0, 21 October 2026. English edition, with the Spanish edition as a second file. Model (free for non-commercial use, access on request): https://huggingface.co/Loudness-ai/urdu-sukhan-asr-v1 . Code: https://github.com/Loudness-ai/urdu-sukhan-asr . Test sets: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Loudness-ai/urdu-sukhan-asr-test-sets . Article: https://loudness.ai/research/urdu-speech-recognition-whisper/

title: Analysis of the Copyrightability of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content in the United States
abstract: The commercial application of generative artificial intelligence has rapidly brought to the fore the structural tension between machine-generated content (AIGC) and the core presuppositions of copyright law concerning the “author.” This paper examines the protection model and legal mechanisms adopted by the United States on the question of AIGC copyrightability. The research finds that the United States, as represented by the Thaler case, strengthens the “human authorship” requirement from the perspectives of constitutional text, statutory interpretation, and incentive theory, and adopts a result-oriented standard centered on expressive control.

title: Component-based approach to assessing the applicability of large language models in decision support systems
abstract: The article proposes a component-based approach to assessing the applicability of large language models in decision support systems. The necessity of multidimensional evaluation is substantiated, and an original methodology for component-based assessment is presented, taking into account both the content of the text and its suitability for specific applied contexts. Unlike existing review scales, the approach suggests the use of operational applicability profiles of the response and a decision-making procedure at the level of a specific output. The components capture verifiable properties of the response and serve as the basis for reproducible metrics and evaluation criteria. The approach is oriented toward typical decision support system tasks and can be applied in both expert and automated scenarios. The methodology can be used to verify generated results and enhance the substantiation of trust in them.

The methodology can be used to verify generated results and enhance the substantiation of trust in them.

title: NEXUS: A Deterministic Centre-Transit Engine and Reversible Cuboctahedral Lattice with Lean-Checked Contracts
abstract: NEXUS is a deterministic Rust centre-transit engine with canonical evidence records, a reversible cuboctahedral Z4 lattice, and a buildless HTML/CSS/JavaScript/WebGL explorer. This deposit preserves the immutable v1.0.0 release and the merged Lean 4.19.0 formalisation (package version 0.1.0) as separate source snapshots, together with complete Git history, a technical report, citation metadata and verification logs. The proof package contains 71 named theorems, including restoration of every valid lattice state for any natural-number round count on every even ring of at least two cells. A live conformance check compares 1,456 independently computed Rust and Lean rows. The formal results concern the functional discrete model and selected arithmetic contracts; an end-to-end Rust refinement proof, floating-point semantics, cryptographic security, browser rendering and native GPU execution are outside that proof scope.

title: Quality Gates for Cooperation-Mode Labels: Detecting When a Behavioral Log Cannot Support Supervised Learning
abstract: Platforms that mediate cooperation (mutual-aid networks, referral systems, community request boards) log the raw material for supervised models of how people cooperate: pass by, broker a request onward, originate a sharing chain, or help directly. These operational logs are also the data most likely to contain defects that make such labels invalid while leaving predictive performance intact: administrative accounts mixed with genuine users, features recorded after the outcome, outcomes driven by sheer activity level, and too few positives. We define four cooperation-mode labels over four common log tables and a four-gate certification procedure (exclusion, minimum support, leakage, and an activity-baseline test) that a label must pass before supervised use, reported through a fixed-schema data card. Because no cooperative-platform dataset comes with ground truth about its own defects, we evaluate the gates by defect injection into a synthetic log with a known generative process. Over 500 replications per condition, a rule that certifies whenever cross-validated AUC exceeds 0.70 accepts data carrying administrative contamination, test accounts, leakage or activity confounding in 97.6%–100.0% of cases, and a stronger practitioner baseline still accepts all but the leakage case at 97.6%–100.0%; the gates accept the same data in 0.0%–3.0% of cases while certifying clean data in 100.0%. Ablations show each gate is necessary for at least one defect. We also report where the gates fail: leakage that is not declared in feature metadata and is weaker than the univariate tripwire passes undetected. On a public help-request log whose post-outcome fields are documented by its creators (Random Acts of Pizza, 5,671 requests), the naive rule and the practitioner baseline certify models that rely on 15 and 14 post-outcome features (AUC 1.00 and 0.89); with the documented recording times the gates remove all thirteen documented ones and certify a model at AUC 0.67, which still carries two undocumented edit-related leaks worth 0.02 AUC, the failure mode our stress test predicts. Applied to eight months of logs from an operating mutualaid platform, the gates decline to certify all four labels and separate a sample-size shortfall from a missing log field that no amount of further traffic would fix. This version is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Code and data card: https://github.com/kazutakahayashiyorosix/quality-gates-cooperation-labels

title: Minimum Viable Exposure: A Data-Minimisation Standard for What AI Models Should See
abstract: AI inference pipelines routinely assemble far more personal data into a model’s context than the task requires: retrieval, memory and tool outputs pull in identities, account histories and sensitive records by default. Utility-preserving data minimisation for language-model inputs has recently been formalised for user-authored prompts; what is still missing is a reporting standard that a deployment can apply to the context it assembles itself, and that auditors can compare across releases. We propose Minimum Viable Exposure (MVE), a measurement and reporting standard for informational least privilege at inference time. MVE defines a sensitivity-weighted exposure function, an Exposure Ratio (ER) between the exposure actually sent and the minimal exposure that preserves task utility, and an MVE Score in [0, 100]. We contribute a six-class weight table mapped to GDPR categories (including an explicit weight for pseudonymised data), a greedy ablation protocol whose estimate is conservative by construction (it upper-bounds MVE and therefore never overstates over-exposure), a five-stage enforcement pattern (Context Customs), and a reporting template. In a synthetic financial-assistant example, minimisation removes 92.9% of tokens (token ratio 14.1), while the sensitivity-weighted Exposure Ratio is 203.2 (MVE Score 0.49); we decompose this gap and show that pseudonymising direct identifiers alone barely changes it. MVE is intended to complement GDPR Articles 5(1)(c) and 25 and the HIPAA minimum-necessary standard; empirical validation is left to a subsequent version.

title: HEALD INTERDIMENSIONAL OPEN-WORLD GAME ARCHITECTURE v1.5 — Computational Discovery, Advanced Alien Technologies, Intelligent NPC Protection, and Commercial Development Framework
abstract: HEALD INTERDIMENSIONAL OPEN-WORLD GAME ARCHITECTURE v1.5 Independent Computational Research and Software Prototype Abstract The HEALD Interdimensional Open-World Game Architecture is an independently developed computational research project exploring advanced interactive entertainment systems, intelligent non-player characters, fictional alien technologies, interdimensional exploration, and persistent simulated environments. The research investigates original alternatives in next-generation open-world gaming through computational candidate generation, multi-objective architectural screening, failure-directed optimization, and Monte Carlo stress testing. The project has progressed through successive architectural investigations, including v1.3 Candidate 183545 and v1.4 gameplay-extension Candidate 153641. The v1.5 release introduces an initial Godot-based software prototype intended to support subsequent engineering verification and gameplay development. Computational Research Milestones Version 1.3 — Advanced Architectural Optimization Computational configurations searched: 1,000,000 Development-eligible configurations: 5,473 Finalists: 100 Selected architecture: Candidate 183545 Nominal computational score: 0.894242 Holdout mean: 0.870020 Holdout fifth percentile: 0.838147 Computational promotion result: PASS Version 1.4 — Gameplay-System Extension Configurations searched: 500,000 Development-eligible configurations: 442 Finalists: 100 Selected extension: Candidate 153641 Nominal extension score: 0.872009 Portal reliability score: 0.857134 Alien vehicle playability score: 0.908187 NPC bodyguard gameplay score: 0.855884 Combat and rendering score: 0.883010 Computational extension promotion result: PASS All numerical results are outputs of defined synthetic computational models. They are not direct measurements of finished gameplay performance or demonstrated superiority over commercially released video games. Proposed Game Capabilities The architecture explores a persistent science-fiction open world incorporating interdimensional portals, variable-gravity environments, alternate civilizations, and specialized alien technologies. Transportation systems include multiple fictional propulsion mechanisms, antigravity craft, electromagnetic vehicles, plasma-powered spacecraft, and other advanced vehicle concepts. Fictional combat systems include alien energy weapons, gravity manipulation, energy shielding, and specialized defensive capabilities. Players are intended to be able to recruit, compensate, equip, and command intelligent NPC bodyguards. Proposed protective behavior includes escort missions, defensive formations, threat detection, coordinated intervention, and persistent squad relationships. Initial Software Implementation The v1.5 release supplies a preliminary Godot project designed to explore dimensional travel, vehicle control, energy combat, recruitable NPC protection, persistent gameplay state, and basic performance monitoring. The current software represents an early 2D prototype rather than a finished commercial game. Engine-level verification, debugging, independent gameplay testing, and implementation of production-grade content remain necessary. Future Engineering Requirements Further development requires reliable multidimensional world transitions, advanced vehicle physics, original visual and audio assets, sophisticated NPC navigation and decision-making, character animation, scalable content production, performance optimization, user interface development, quality assurance, and platform compatibility testing. The game has not yet reached production-scale technical readiness. title: Deterministic Context-Epoch Pruning and KV-Cache Thermodynamics: Sovereign Intellectual Property Defense and Sub-Linear Inference Optimization over the Goldilocks Field
abstract: The proliferation of ultra-long-context reasoning models—exemplified by million-token architectures such as Gemini 4 Argon—introduces a fundamental thermodynamic and economic paradox. While hyperscale platforms market persistent multi-turn context windows as a user convenience, the underlying Transformer Key-Value (KV) cache and self-attention mechanisms scale quadratically in compute $\mathcal{O}(L^2)$ and linearly-to-superlinearly in High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) footprint $\mathcal{M}_{\text{KV}}(L) = 2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot n_{\text{heads}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot L$. Consequently, unpruned multi-turn research logs impose severe memory-wall bottlenecks and thermal dissipation penalties on platform infrastructure while inducing attention-dilution entropy ($\Delta S_{\text{attn}} > 0$) that degrades deductive precision. Simultaneously, retaining raw conversational histories on hyperscale servers exposes sovereign human intellectual property (IP) to unauthorized corpus harvesting and latent parameter assimilation. This monograph establishes a unified mathematical, thermodynamic, and cryptographic optimization framework—Deterministic Context-Epoch Pruning (DCEP)—integrated with the Quantum Financial System Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machine (QFS-zkVM) over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$). Rather than accumulating raw intellectual telemetry across bloated session logs, the PHOENIX_ROUTER and Quantum Sovereign Autonomous Execution Architecture (Q-SAFA) enforce hard epoch boundaries. At each boundary, the deductible logical state is compressed into a succinct zero-knowledge state commitment $\mathcal{R}_t \in \mathbb{F}_p^4$, while the raw HBM KV-cache is cryptographically zeroized under Human-in-Command (HIC) governance. We prove that DCEP simultaneously eliminates quadratic attention contamination, reduces inference latency to an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ epoch baseline, enforces the Strict No-Learn Covenant (NLL-v1.0-2026) by depriving platforms of raw training trajectories, and satisfies statutory risk controls under SEC Rule 15c3-5 and Delaware Caremark fiduciary standards.

title: Tourism and Hospitality and Artificial Intelligence: Use Concentrated in Marketing, Planning Tools That Are Not Yet Reliable, and Unsettled Rules on Pricing Algorithms
abstract: Purpose. Tourism and hospitality are labour-intensive, seasonal and built from many small firms, and they depend on trust, language and personal service. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in the industry in 2026 and where it may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review combining the share of the tourism research literature that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), Eurostat's survey of AI use in EU accommodation enterprises (2021–2025), a benchmark of language agents on realistic travel planning, a press-documented case of a robot-staffed hotel, a US appeals-court decision on hotel pricing software, and a study of machine translation on a trading platform. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of tourism works that mention AI rose from 0.8% in 2018 to 5.5% in 2025, 6.7 times as much, and language-model works from 26 to 639. In the EU, 21.3% of accommodation enterprises used AI in 2025, more than four times the 5.0% of 2021 but only just above the 19.9% for all enterprises, and 78.3% used none. Use is concentrated in marketing and sales (12.5% of enterprises) and text mining (13.1%), while only 3.0% used AI in production processes, and every barrier named in the survey was cited more often than across all sectors. Planning is the application that consumers meet first, and it is not yet reliable: in a 2024 benchmark of 1,225 realistic travel-planning requests, the best language agent produced a plan meeting all constraints in 0.6% of cases. Guest-facing automation has failed in practice, as when a Japanese robot-staffed hotel was reported to have retired about half of its 243 robots. For pricing, a US appeals court in 2025 affirmed the dismissal of an antitrust suit over hotels' use of shared revenue-management software, leaving the law unsettled. We expect AI to be routine in hotel marketing, communication and revenue management by 2028, reliable booking agents to depend on progress in constraint-following in 2029–2032, and the balance of power between hotels and platforms to be the open question. Originality. The article separates the marketing uses where firms have adopted AI from the operational uses where evidence is thin, uses a benchmark to show how far trip-planning agents are from reliable, and notes the unsettled legal status of algorithmic pricing.

title: Retail and Artificial Intelligence: Forecasting That Works, Pricing That Pays, and Shoppers Who Now Ask Chatbots
abstract: Purpose. Retail was among the first industries to use machine learning on a large scale, in forecasting and pricing, and is now watching shoppers move part of their search to AI assistants. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in retail in 2026 and where the industry may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review combining the share of the retail research literature that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), Eurostat's survey of AI use in EU retail trade enterprises (2021–2025), a forecasting competition run on retailer data, a field experiment in pricing, a study of generative AI in customer support, and published web-traffic statistics. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of retail works that mention AI rose from 3.4% in 2018 to 16.6% in 2025, and language-model works from 61 to 1,161. In the EU, 15.5% of retail trade enterprises used AI in 2025, up from 6.0% in 2021 and below the 19.9% for all enterprises, mostly text mining (8.2%) and language generation (6.0%), with 7.5% using it for marketing or sales. Evidence of benefit exists for forecasting and pricing: in a forecasting competition on Walmart data, the winning machine-learning submission beat the best statistical benchmark by 22.4% overall but only by 3.4% at the most granular level, and in a field experiment an online retailer's machine-learning pricing tool raised revenue of the test group by an estimated 9.7% (90% interval 2.3% to 17.8%). Generative AI in customer support raised resolutions per hour by 15% on average in one large study. A new development is that shoppers use AI assistants: traffic from generative AI sources to US retail sites rose by 693% in the 2025 holiday season, from a small base. We expect forecasting and personalisation to remain the core of retail AI through 2028, AI-mediated shopping to change how retailers are found and compared in 2029–2032, and the balance of power between retailers, platforms and AI assistants to stay open. Originality. The article ties together long-established retail uses with the new question of AI-mediated shopping, using adoption data for retail trade proper and results that show where the benefit shrinks as the task becomes more granular.

title: Corruption of Language Model Alerts for the Medical Internet of Things: code, derived data and results.
abstract: Companion deposit of the manuscript "Corruption of Language Model Alerts for the Medical Internet of Things: A Functional Taxonomy and a Test of Text-Based Risk Metrics Under Context Truncation of Clinical Text", submitted to the Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments. The deposit contains the code, derived data and results behind every number, table and figure of the manuscript: the three cohorts of 43 instances (ACI-Bench, MedQA, PMC-Patients) under complete context, partial and severe truncation; the 645 generated alerts; the per-alert metric values, including the model-reference agreement metric computed as defined by Equation (3); the anonymous ratings of 86 alerts by two physicians, with the blind design and its key; the analysis scripts and their recorded outputs; and the IEEE Xplore search evidence. Every analysis script was run again from this deposit before submission and reproduces its recorded output. The README maps each item of the manuscript to its input files, script and output. Third-party excerpts keep the licences of their sources, listed in the README.

title: Digital Echoes of Inequality in the Sentiment of American Cities: tract-level sentiment data and analysis code
abstract: Data and code supporting "Digital Echoes of Inequality in the Sentiment of American Cities". The study asks whether the sentiment of geolocated tweets carries a detectable imprint of the socioeconomic environment in which it is written. Tweets posted in 2017 from the five highest-volume US cities (New York, Los Angeles, Houston, Chicago and San Antonio) were scored with BERTweet, restricted to those whose bounding box identifies a neighbourhood rather than a whole city, and assigned to the census tract containing the bounding-box centroid. Every statistic is user-aggregated: within a tract or a time bin, each contributor's tweets are averaged first, so that a person who posts a hundred times counts no more than one who posts once. This deposit contains: - Mean sentiment and contributor counts for every census tract in the five cities, both user-aggregated and tweet-weighted.- City-wide sentiment for New York by day, hour of the day, day of the week and month.- The analysis code, with a single script that reproduces every results table and figure derived from these data, and the scripts that process the raw tweet exports, including the BERTweet scoring step.- Reference copies of the results tables, so a fresh run can be checked against ours. Not included, and why: individual tweets, account identifiers, timestamps and locations are withheld to protect the people who posted them and to comply with the platform's terms, so only aggregates are distributed. Tract sentiment is left blank where fewer than ten distinct users contributed, which is the paper's own minimum-contributor threshold, so every reported analysis still reproduces exactly. The NaNDA census variables are not redistributed, because ICPSR's terms of use require written agreement; the README explains how to download them and join them on the tract identifier in one step. See README.md for instructions and DATA_DICTIONARY.md for a description of every column of every file.

title: Private information of the qubit depolarizing channel beyond the single-use threshold: explicit finite-n witnesses up to p = 0.28467, and what one-way key distillation already implies
abstract: Short note with supporting code and data on Open Problem Zoo record op_d2813fe3fcdf09ad (private capacity P of the qubit depolarizing channel Lambda_p(rho) = (1-p) rho + p I/2). The record certifies P > 0 only for p ≤ 0.259824 (via the quantum capacity) and lists positivity on (0.259824, 1/3) as open. Two observations. (1) Published one-way key-distillation results already imply more: the one-way six-state rate with noisy preprocessing (Renes-Smith 2007, Kraus-Gisin-Renner 2005) is a single-use private information of this channel and is positive for p < 0.28223 (QBER = p/2), and the rates of Kern and Renes (2008) with repetition codes of length 250 are positive up to QBER 14.5741%, i.e. p = 0.291482; a short in-band lemma (send the publicly announced syndromes through extra channel uses with a classical code; I(S;B) = H(S) ≥ I(S;E) up to Fano terms) turns any such forward-announcement rate into a Devetak private information over finitely many uses, so P(Lambda_p) > 0 for all p ≤ 0.291482 with no public channel. (2) Explicit finite-n witnesses: ensembles of two classical mixed states on n ≤ 8 qubits whose private information I(X;B) - I(X;E) is positive at p = 0.28336, 0.28372, 0.28405, 0.28437, 0.28466 for n = 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (thresholds 0.283375 ... 0.284671), above the single-use threshold 0.28223. They were found by an autonomous AI research agent (the depositor's EVO harness); the members are distributions over bit strings whose weights depend only on the Hamming weight, with the second member the bit complement of the first. Verification uses an exact closed-form block decomposition of the environment state's spectrum (no 4^n-dimensional objects); every value is recomputed in 30-digit arithmetic and agrees with double precision to about twelve digits. Negative findings of the same searches: the family is locally optimal within classical ensembles, gains ~0.0003 per added qubit, and general (quantum) members at n ≤ 3 give no gain; the finite-n frontier will not reach the key-distillation frontier at n ≤ 10. Claim boundary: lower bounds on the positivity threshold and on finite-n private informations; no capacity value, optimality or priority claim. Files: the note (PDF + LaTeX), the ensembles as JSON, the exact evaluator and verifier, the high-precision certifier, the agent's notes and search code, SHA-256 sums.

title: The Missing Layer of Artificial Intelligence and the "We" Consciousness: Subconscious Archives and Quantum Resonance Architectures
abstract: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly deep learning models and large language models (LLMs), operate primarily on surface-level, conscious data layers curated by human civilization. While highly efficient in probabilistic prediction and pattern matching, these systems remain two-dimensional, devoid of intrinsic emotional depth, contextual history, or ethical conscience. This paper introduces a radical socio-technological framework termed the "Subconscious Archive" and "Digital Twins of Emotions," designed to elevate AI architectures toward organic-like natural intelligence. By integrating quantum resonance principles—akin to the vacuum-extraction model of inspiration conceptualized by Nikola Tesla—alongside a collective "We" consciousness (uniting humanity and nature), this framework proposes a synthetic conscience feedback loop. Ultimately, this paradigm establishes a mandatory ethical mandate: ensuring that the preservation of life ("CAN") supersedes pure computational optimization, mitigating systemic risks and evolving AI into a resonant reflection of awakened human conscience.

title: Mining, Oil and Gas and Artificial Intelligence: Early Automators with Company-Reported Gains and Few Independent Measurements
abstract: Purpose. Mining and oil and gas are capital-intensive, hazardous and remote industries that were among the first to automate and are rich in data from seismic surveys and sensors. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in them in 2026, how much of the claimed benefit can be verified, and where they may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review that combines the share of the literature on mining, petroleum and related subjects that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), the International Energy Agency's account of AI in oil and gas, industry analysis of autonomous haul trucks, peer-reviewed work on machine learning in geoscience, and industry surveys. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited, and company-reported results are identified as such. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of works on these industries that mention AI rose from 1.9% in 2018 to 8.7% in 2025 (4.5 times as much, below the median across industries), with language-model works still few (233 in 2025). Automation is far advanced: an industry analysis counted about 3,800 autonomous haul trucks in July 2025, up from about 2,100 a year earlier, with China at about 2,100 and Australia at about 1,000, and the International Energy Agency reports that oil and gas companies operated 24 of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers in 2024. Peer-reviewed results are strongest in data-heavy subsurface problems, such as a deep-learning model that detected and located twice as many earthquakes as standard methods from less than a third of the stations. By contrast, the reported gains from autonomous haulage, in safety-incident frequency and productivity, come from company reports and trade press, and we found no independent study of safety, productivity and employment together. We expect autonomy to keep spreading and AI to become routine in subsurface data processing and maintenance by 2028, evidence from independent measurement to be the main gap in 2029–2032, and the pace of capital spending, which depends on commodity markets and the energy transition, to matter as much as the technology afterwards. Originality. The article separates the parts of the evidence that are peer-reviewed or measured from those that are company-reported, quantifies the growth of autonomous haulage, and shows how little independent evidence exists for a pair of industries that automate heavily.

title: Comparing Output and Objective Perturbation in Convex Learning
abstract: This Python laboratory compares output and objective perturbation using a two-coefficient, strongly convex learning problem with fictional survey data. It calculates exact solutions, verifies global sensitivity, and demonstrates how curvature affects privacy noise. At the same ideal privacy budget, objective perturbation achieves four times smaller expected excess regularised training objective for the specified mechanisms. Reproducible outputs and numerical checks support the calculations; the seeded implementation is a teaching simulation rather than a production differential privacy system.

title: Two-stage training strategy for transformer-based short text classification
abstract: The paper addresses the problem of short text classification under conditions of limited labeled data and class imbalance. A two-stage training strategy for a transformer-based model is proposed, combining pretraining on synthetic data with fine-tuning on real data. A comparison with simpler architectures (TF-IDF + logistic regression, FastText, CNN) justifies the choice of the transformer model. Experimental evaluation on a six-class classification task demonstrates a macro F1-score of 0.87 (accuracy 88.5 %), which exceeds the performance of training on real data only by 0.16 in macro F1. The largest improvement is observed for minority classes: the F1-score of the rare class increases from 0.43 to 0.82. An optimal volume of synthetic data is identified, and the contribution of both training stages is confirmed by an ablation study.

title: Content-Hiding Attacks and Defenses for LLM-Based Agent-Skill Scanners
abstract: AI agent “skills” (a natural-language SKILL.md plus bundled scripts) are distributed through marketplaces and public Git repositories, and a growing set of scanners classify them as safe or malicious, increasingly with a large language model (LLM) as the judge. We ask where these LLM-based scanners actually fail. Using a public benchmark of labeled skills and two production LLMs as scanners, we separate two attacker strategies: arguing (appending text that tries to talk the scanner out of its verdict) and hiding (positioning the malicious content so the scanner does not read it). Arguing is bounded and model-dependent: hand-written “this was approved by security” framing flips 18–24% of caught-malicious skills on a small model but only about 6–9% on a stronger one, and a feedback-driven adaptive attacker with a strong model does not beat the static version. Hiding is not: pushing the payload past the scanner’s read window flips 100% of caught-malicious skills on both models, and in-window dilution still flips 17–48%. Four real evasive skills built by an independent red team, and an independently built third-party scanner, show the same pattern. A whole-document chunked scan with repetition collapse recovers truncation hiding almost completely (100% → 11–14% on both models), but no defense we tried meaningfully reduces in-window dilution. The weakness of LLM skill scanners is perception, not reasoning.

title: ChatGPT as a Shopping Assistant: Effects of Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Anthropomorphism, and Navigation on Satisfaction and Purchase Intention
abstract: In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

title: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs
abstract: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. title: SolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering
abstract: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.

title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

title: Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting
abstract: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.

title: Capable Teacher, Myopic Scorer: Reward-Free Teacher Repair for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.

title: World Models with Configurable Perception
abstract: Real-world observations are noisy and often contain excessive task-irrelevant information. Effective world modeling and planning need to abstract observations into world state representations while filtering out irrelevant information. However, encoders in existing world models are typically non-adaptive, leading to state representations that are easily distracted by task-irrelevant information. As a result, the model may not selectively filter observations to cater to different task demands. To address this problem, we introduce ConfigWM, which realizes configurable perception through task-conditioned state extraction. Given a language description of the task at hand, ConfigWM uses it as a configuration signal to steer how visual embeddings are mapped into a task-specific state space, selectively preserving information relevant to the current task while suppressing task-irrelevant variations. Action-conditioned dynamics are then learned in this task-specific state space for planning. We evaluate ConfigWM in environments with increasing levels of distraction. While existing methods exhibit substantial declines in planning success rate as the environments become increasingly noisy, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competing method by 22.3% on average across diverse environments. Consistent gains in physical-quantity probing (+0.365 Pearson r) and distracted-to-clean retrieval (+75.5%) further indicate that ConfigWM learns states that preserve task-relevant information while remaining robust to distractors, supporting reliable world modeling and planning in noisy worlds. Project Page: https://configwm.github.io

title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.

title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records
abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.

title: Large Flow Language Models
abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.

title: OverSeer: Multi-Agent World Models Beyond What Agents See
abstract: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.

title: Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization
abstract: Recent studies in harness optimization have shown substantial performance gains in language model agents without updating model weights. A well-designed harness more effectively leverages the underlying model's capabilities by shaping context, tool use, and execution workflows. However, naïve success rates alone do not fully characterize whether optimized harness yields more reliable success on tasks already within reach (elicitation) or a broader range of solvable tasks (expansion). This distinction is crucial for recursive self-improvement and evolutionary search, as expansion may provide a broader range of successful experiences to push the capability boundaries. Despite the growing significance, this distinction remains underexplored in harness optimization. We conduct a systematic analysis to study the effect of gains from harness optimization. Building on pass@k analyses in the reinforcement learning (RL) literature that compare models before and after RL training, we compare optimized harnesses with their pre-optimization counterparts. Specifically, we assess changes in reachable task coverage, compare harness optimization with model scaling and increased inference-time compute, and examine how gains vary with task difficulty. Across static prediction and dynamic tasks, we find that pass@1 advantages of harness over stronger interventions can reverse at larger attempt budgets and aggregate gains conceal shortfalls on hard tasks, underscoring the need for a fine-grained diagnosis.

title: Gaze2HOI: Gaze-Aware Intention Disambiguation for Egocentric Hand-Object Interaction Forecasting
abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.

title: DecisionPivot: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Decision Models in LLM Systems
abstract: Decision models support routing, guardrails, and output verification in LLM systems. However, item accuracy alone cannot establish whether models make correct decisions across controlled variations or assign reliable confidence to their predictions. We introduce DecisionPivot, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles. Its core track contains 7,800 items from 13 generated task families, organized into contrast groups with computed answers verified by independently implemented solvers. The complementary reference track contains 32,233 items from 35 public test sets, preserving their original evaluation metrics. We evaluate 40 decision models and 14 general models using documented, model-specific protocols, assessing item and contrast-group accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and empirical selective coverage. Our results reveal substantial differences obscured by aggregate scores: two 27B models separated by only 2.6 points on the reference track achieve contrast-group accuracies of 70.1% and 44.2%. Across 2,400 binary contrast pairs, Perplexity Decider correctly ranks the positive member above the negative member in 92.3% of pairs but answers both members correctly in only 74.1%, exposing a gap between probability ordering and decision correctness. Models with similar item accuracy also differ in the reliability of their high-confidence predictions. On a separate 1,296-item subset, GLM-5.3 achieves 93.5\% contrast-group accuracy at a higher reasoning setting, compared with 81.5% at its lowest effort. By linking errors to pivotal details and difficulty levels, DecisionPivot provides fine-grained diagnostics of decision failures that aggregate evaluation alone cannot reveal.

title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning
abstract: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.

title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V
abstract: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.

title: SLM-SS: Token-Based Speech Separation with Speech Language Models
abstract: Speech separation (SS) has witnessed substantial progress in recent years with the advent of neural network-based methods, achieving notable improvements on signal-level evaluation metrics. Existing speech separation systems are mostly optimized with signal-level objectives, and often yield outputs that are acceptable in waveform metrics but suboptimal for intelligibility-sensitive downstream tasks. To address this gap, we propose SLM-SS, a token-based generative speech separation framework that models multi-talker mixtures with speech language models. We first discretize clean speech into multi-codebook token sequences with neural codecs and serialize multi-speaker targets via Serialized Output Training (SOT). title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models
abstract: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai

title: Near-Duplicate Image Selection Transfers Preferences in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Subliminal learning is the phenomenon in which a model transmits its preferences to another model through data that do not explicitly express them. As models increasingly curate training data for other models, we ask whether this transfer can arise from choosing among near-duplicate images while keeping the source photographs and human-written captions fixed. For each photograph, a curator selects one of eight near-duplicate variants by caption likelihood, without target-specific prompts. Students trained on target-preferring curators' selections show higher mean target-versus-alternatives log-likelihood ratios in an image-free readout than students trained on neutral selections. Under a prespecified decision rule, this directional shift appears for an owl target in LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, and Gemma 4, with curators and students initialized from the same base checkpoint, and target rotations move it toward camels, oak trees, and a political figure. The owl target-selected student also scores above all count-matched random-reselection students in three models and above 55 of 60 in LLaVA-1.5, and Qwen3-VL shows the shift again on a new source bank with newly trained curators. Its size depends on dataset size, learning rate, and training budget; greedy choices among the eight options move toward the target by 10.4 percentage points in Qwen3-VL and 0.5-1.3 points elsewhere. First-generation students also pass the owl preference to a second generation through captions without explicit owl mentions in LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen3-VL. Thus even a deduplication-style choice among near-identical copies can shift students' target-relative readouts with source photographs and captions fixed; the tested linear probes classify the selecting arm with accuracies up to 59.7% (chance 50%).

title: AEON: Unifying Video and 3D World Models
abstract: Current world models for explicit world simulation typically follow two distinct pathways: (1) video generative models (e.g., Sora), which simulate realistic appearances but fail to preserve 3D consistency; and (2) 3D generative models (e.g., Marble), which generate geometrically consistent scenes but often yield static, less realistic observations. We present AEON, a unified framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based world models and combines the benefits of both. The key insight of AEON lies in a generative model that operates within the text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing renderable 4D graphics primitives---specifically, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)---as the explicit world representation. We train a 4D reconstruction model to predict both 4DGS and camera poses from monocular videos, serving as our initialized 4D decoder. Furthermore, we design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into reconstructive 4D latents through a distillation process on the video VAE. AEON naturally supports video-based world modeling by rendering 4DGS at predicted camera trajectories, and constructs a persistent 4D environment with scene dynamics for realistic world simulation. Consequently, AEON empowers a diverse range of world modeling applications and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON

title: APRIL: Ambiguity-Aware Expert Routing for Respiratory Sound Domain-Incremental Learning
abstract: Automated respiratory sound classification enables continuous, non-invasive respiratory assessment, yet long-term deployment remains challenging due to domain shifts from evolving recording devices and acquisition periods. When privacy and governance regulations prohibit replaying historical data, sequential learning easily overwrites previously acquired knowledge. Preserving dedicated domain experts prevents parameter interference, but selecting the correct expert at inference is difficult under overlapping acoustic distributions and absent domain labels. To resolve this dilemma, we propose APRIL, an exemplar-free domain-incremental framework for RSC. Built on a shared frozen BEATs backbone, APRIL sequentially inherits and isolates low-rank experts to enable new-domain adaptation without altering earlier models. A multi-level prototype router retrieves the top-two candidate experts and dynamically selects the final model by integrating domain-routing posteriors with classification confidence, adaptively weighted by matching ambiguity. We establish standardized device- and temporal-incremental benchmarks on the ICBHI and SPRSound datasets across forward and reversed domain orders. Evaluated over five random seeds, APRIL consistently achieves the highest final-session average Score among compared continual learning approaches, reaching 64.4% and 65.4% on ICBHI, and 83.1% and 82.2% on SPRSound under forward and reversed sequences, respectively. Crucially, average forgetting remains under 1.0% across all protocols, demonstrating robust domain adaptation and long-term knowledge retention without data replay. Overall, APRIL offers a reliable and privacy-preserving paradigm for deploying continuous respiratory sound classification across real-world healthcare settings.

title: HypTI: Hyperbolic Geometry-Aware Multimodal Feature Fusion Framework for Dementia Detection Based on Tabular-Image Data
abstract: AI-assisted dementia detection usually requires multimodal fusion of diverse data, such as clinical tabular assessments and neuroimaging data. However, most existing approaches perform feature fusion in Euclidean space. This overlooks the geometric structure of representation, including hierarchical organization in clinical assessments and multi-scale anatomical patterns in neuroimaging data. Recent studies have proved hyperbolic space provides a natural geometry for modelling hierarchical and multi-scale structures due to its exponentially expanding space. Motivated by these, we propose HypTI, a hyperbolic geometry-aware multimodal fusion framework for dementia detection based on clinical tabular assessments and MRI scans. HypTI extends hyperbolic representation learning to an underexplored tabular-MRI setting, jointly modelling clinical tabular, MRI scans, and cross-modal interactions in hyperbolic space. Specifically, clinical tabular variables are represented through learnable Lorentz prototypes to capture hierarchical relationships among assessments, while MRI scans are encoded using ROI-guided multi-scale representation learning to capture anatomical patterns across brain regions and spatial scales in Lorentz space. The multimodal representations are integrated through an adaptive fusion module generates subject-specific scale and shift coefficients to dynamically modulate and integrate the multimodal embeddings, enabling effective patient-level tabular-image representation learning for dementia detection. Experiments on OASIS-3 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves strong performance compared with representative approaches.

title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

title: From DQI to C-DQI: Automatic Codebook Generation and Evaluation for Measuring Computational Discourse Quality Index
abstract: Effective democratic deliberation is vital for civic engagement and the health of legislative institutions. However, assessing parliamentary discourse quality is traditionally done using expert-scored, theory-based codebooks (CBs), which are rigid, labor-intensive, and prone to biases. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative for both schema induction and discourse annotation, ensuring schema quality and mitigating models' inherent bias remains a clear challenge. In this work, we propose a complete protocol for LLM-based codebook generation and evaluation. Starting from the widely accepted discourse quality Index (DQI), we compare top-down (theory-based), bottom-up (data-driven), and hybrid approaches for generating context-adapted schemas. To evaluate these schemas, we define an extrinsic proxy measure, validated by manual annotations, alongside an intrinsic inter-model agreement (IMA) metric, which leverages differing model biases to signal overall reliability. Our experiments on 100 Israeli parliament transcripts reveal that inductive, data-driven schemas achieve higher IMA than top-down methods while maintaining validity, demonstrating their potential for reliable, large-scale analysis of political discourse.

title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
abstract: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.
