title: Orebody Knowledge From Calculated Mineralogy, GRE46 Gold Deposit, Australia
abstract: The Cowal Gold Operation in central New South Wales (Australia) has recently commenced production from the underground GRE46 gold deposit. GRE46 is expected to contribute a significant portion of the site's future gold production, which was previously derived exclusively from the E42 open pit. This new, more variable ore-type introduces additional complexity to the processing circuit. Deposit-scale quantification of the mineralogical variability that underpins rock physio-chemical behaviour during the extraction cycle is therefore a critical aspect of orebody knowledge that reduces uncertainty and technical risk. In this study we demonstrate a workflow to develop, refine and subsequently verify a spatially constrained three-dimensional calculated mineralogy model for GRE46 that can be used to correlate with comminution characteristics that may influence the processing performance. Here we present the results of two element-to-mineral conversion models using common multi-element geochemical assays with increasing levels of geological input, and compare the calculated mineralogy to mineralogy data determined by X-ray diffraction. The initial model adopts nominal end member and stoichiometric mineral compositions, while the refined model incorporates domain-specific mineral solid solution compositions for chlorite and white mica measured by laser ablation inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry. The accuracy of predicted white mica and chlorite content is improved substantially between the initial and refined models relative to the measured X-ray diffraction data (white mica R 2 0.61 initial vs 0.90 refined ; chlorite R 2 0.3 initial vs 0.67 refined ). This work highlights the importance of appropriate geochemical domaining and mineral solid solution chemistry on the predictive accuracy for several bulk minerals at GRE46.

title: Beyond Omni: A Unified MLLM for Embodied Sensory Understanding
abstract: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.

title: Gradient descent reaches arbitrary accuracy in a fixed number of large steps on multiclass logistic regression
abstract: We show that gradient descent (GD) with step size $η$ can achieve $\varepsilon$ optimality gap on the multiclass logistic regression loss in a number of iterations $T$ that is independent of $\varepsilon$. To do so, the step size $η$ must be chosen large enough as a function of $\varepsilon$ (and properties of the linearly separable dataset), while $T$ is a constant that only depends on the data. The relevant properties of the data include the number of points and their margin (for $T$), and one additional quantity (for $η$) that turns out to be necessary in dimension $d \geq 3$. The proofs build on the known fact that, as $η\to \infty$, suitably rescaled GD becomes the perceptron algorithm, and the latter finds a perfect classifier in $T$ iterations. A similar claim was shown for two classes in dimension $d = 2$ using other proof techniques. This result adds to previous works that showed GD on the logistic regression loss can be accelerated by taking large step sizes. Those provoke a wild, oscillatory initial phase, followed by a stable phase. We provide results of this (qualitatively different) nature, too.

title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

title: Polar Switch: Fast Muon Orthogonalization with Polynomial Circuits
abstract: Muon, a 2024-born optimizer for language models, differs from the 2015-born spectral gradient descent mainly in its fast, GPU-friendly Newton--Schulz polynomial for orthogonalizing the gradient matrix. Accordingly, a line of research proposes faster polynomial iterations for gradient orthogonalization, such as Polar Express and Gram Newton--Schulz, both built on quintic polynomials. In this paper, we introduce Polar Switch, a new approach to polynomial gradient orthogonalization. Using simple polynomial circuits, Polar Switch reaches a given high polynomial degree at a lower FLOP cost than quintic iterations. We define a circuit as a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a few square buffers, and circuits with $k$ products form a restricted family of odd polynomials of degree up to $2^{k+1}+1$. We choose the sequence of products in each circuit, their coefficients, and how the circuits are composed by numerically minimizing a worst-case bound on the polar approximation error. This minimization is subject to a FLOP budget that accounts for symmetric matrix multiplication kernels and a rounding constraint for numerical stability in half precision. title: Native Real-Time Interactive Omni Intelligence: A Unified Framework
abstract: The rapid progress of large language models has established strong foundations for reasoning, knowledge, and generation, while the integration of vision, audio, video, and other modalities has extended these capabilities toward increasingly unified intelligence across modalities, which we refer to as Omni Intelligence. Yet, real-world assistants must do more than process completed multimodal prompts. They must perceive evolving streams, respond while new evidence is arriving, handle hesitation, overlap, interruption, and changing intent, and coordinate reasoning or tool use that may proceed asynchronously. We refer to this broader capability as \( \textbf{Interactive Omni Intelligence} \): the ability to maintain and exercise omni intelligence under the temporal and adaptive demands of real-time interaction. The question guiding this paper is: How can foundation-model capabilities be carried into real-time interaction while preserving both intelligence and interactivity?We develop a conceptual framework connecting two development paths. One adapts pretrained language or omni models through streaming interfaces, modality modules, post-training, and orchestration. The other develops model-native systems that learn temporal structure, continuous multimodal processing, generation, and interaction control. Across both paths, we compare representations, architectures, fusion, data, training objectives, serving, and evaluation. Their comparison reveals an Intelligence--Interactivity Trade-off between preserving reasoning and knowledge, and meeting the timing, coordination, and resource demands of continuous operation. We examine Multi-Rate Interactive Intelligence as a cross-cutting direction, including foreground--background designs that coordinate fast interaction with slower reasoning, retrieval, memory, and tools. Finally, we identify open problems in evolving state, persistent and proactive interaction, joint evaluation, and safe open-world operation. The resulting framework connects capability preservation, interaction control, and multi-rate coordination.

title: CheckDistill: Adaptive Checklist Distillation for Efficient Distributional Reward Modeling in Image Editing
abstract: Reinforcement learning for instruction-guided image editing requires reward models that provide reliable, accurate, and efficient feedback. Direct scalar prediction compresses multidimensional editing preferences, whereas generative evaluators can expose their judgment through explicit reasoning. However, broad scoring criteria do not specify all instance-dependent editing and preservation constraints, and generating long reasoning trajectories is costly for online optimization. We introduce CheckDistill, a pointwise reward modeling framework that internalizes instruction-adaptive checklists. We decompose each editing condition into atomic, independently verifiable requirements and construct four-dimensional scoring labels together with structured verification evidence. After supervised score initialization, a privileged teacher conditions on checklists, item-level judgments, and dimension-level rationales to supervise the student's own scoring trajectories. A reliability-weighted on-policy self-distillation objective adjusts supervision at score tokens according to agreement between the teacher's expected scores and reference labels, while retaining candidate probability weights in a truncated token support. The deployed student directly predicts four score distributions without checklist inputs or explicit reasoning and aggregates their expectations into a scalar reward. CheckDistill achieves aggregate accuracies of 72.30%, 56.67% and 82.90% on MMRB2, MER-Bench and EditReward-Bench, respectively, exceeding the compared open-source baselines on all three metrics.

title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation
abstract: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.

title: Towards understanding dynamic relationships within large corpus’ of social content.
abstract: This dissertation describes methods of answering attitude questions and building descriptions of representative authors from a large corpus of news comments. These approaches are then expanded to develop a method of generating a network-shaped summary of online social content. This network-shaped summary is a human-interpretable output describing the discussions occurring within the content (specifically, large set of user comments discussing online news articles). This output takes the form of an annotated network, where nodes represent a small set of possible, representative authors within the body of comments, and edges represent possible arguments between these representative, or ‘prototypical’ authors. The result is a ‘prototype relation network’, with text content on the nodes and edges. These networks can be used as features for downstream tasks by embedding the text content, and utilizing learned graph processing operations within prediction models. This dissertation outlines and evaluates the process of generating these networks, and outlines methods of generating features from the networks for downstream tasks, using the example application of social media popularity prediction.

title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
abstract: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

title: Distance-based Empirical Bayes: a nonparametric B-spline approach
abstract: Empirical Bayes methods estimate a prior distribution from repeated observations and use it to construct posterior inference, but nonparametric approaches based on marginal likelihood maximization often produce discrete mixing distributions and can be numerically unstable or poorly calibrated when the true prior is continuous, heavy-tailed, skewed, or multimodal. This dissertation develops an Integral Probability Metric Empirical Bayes (IPM-EB) framework for one-dimensional latent priors. The unknown prior is represented as a nonnegative B-spline density satisfying an explicit normalization constraint, and its coefficients are estimated by matching the empirical marginal distribution of the data to the model-implied marginal distribution using either the Maximum Mean Discrepancy or the standard 1-Wasserstein distance. Likelihood-aware knot placement allows the same construction to be used across Gaussian, Poisson, Binomial, Gamma, and Weibull observation models without reducing all problems to a Gaussian working likelihood. We prove weak consistency of the idealized prior estimator under an expanding-sieve framework, with metric specific conditions for MMD and W1, and show that the induced empirical Bayes posterior is weakly consistent at fixed observation values. Simulation studies across seven likelihood families show that IPM-EB generally provides competitive posterior mean accuracy while improving continuous prior recovery and uncertainty calibration, particularly in heavy-tailed, skewed, multimodal, and scale/shape settings. In two baseball applications, including the Efron–Morris benchmark and a large 2002–2012 MLB batting dataset, IPM-EB achieves strong predictive accuracy while maintaining interpretable continuous prior estimates. These results suggest that IPM-based distribution matching offers a robust and flexible alternative to likelihood-based nonparametric empirical Bayes estimation.

title: EpiLens: Lightweight RAG for Epidemiological Knowledge Acquisition
abstract: To prepare for future outbreaks, researchers need to know what studies have been done and what data they use. Mapping a large literature by hand is slow, while large language models alone can misstate or conflate sources. We present EpiLens, a lightweight, open-source retrieval-augmented generation package that applies a fixed retrieval template and output schema to every paper in a corpus and links outputs to source passages. We build a corpus of 2,297 papers from the sources of a multi-pathogen parameter study and evaluate EpiLens's paper-classification workflow against 214 manually labelled papers. Without task-specific training data, the classifier matches or exceeds the tested supervised and zero-shot baselines across four tasks. The study's early extraction sheets cite published sources for 327 estimates. We link each estimate to a cited document or to corpus studies included by a review. Then, we use the classifier's labels to compare the papers associated with different parameters and pathogens. EpiLens labels more papers linked to reproduction numbers than fatality risks as model-based (54% versus 22%, compared with 62% versus 24% in the manual labels). The gap is consistent with the frequent use of transmission models to estimate reproduction numbers and persists within each of five pathogens compared. Beyond the contrast between parameters, the model-based share of papers linked to incubation-period estimates differs by pathogen: 55% for SARS-CoV-2 versus 6% for mpox.

title: Predictive modeling using heterogeneous data sources
abstract: The increasing availability of heterogeneous data has transformed the scope and capabilities of predictive modeling across scientific, social, and environmental domains. Modern predictive systems no longer rely on a single structured dataset collected under controlled conditions. Instead, relevant information is distributed across multiple modalities, platforms, temporal scales, and relational structures. Social media interactions generate large volumes of unstructured textual and network data that reflect human behavior and collective attention. Environmental monitoring systems produce high-dimensional geospatial and temporal measurements describing weather patterns, soil properties, and ecological conditions. Scientific repositories and digital libraries contain rapidly growing collections of publications, metadata, and domain-specific representations that require automated extraction and organization. These heterogeneous sources provide substantial predictive potential, but they also introduce significant methodological challenges related to data integration, representation learning, scalability, and generalization. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful framework for extracting predictive signals from such complex data environments. However, conventional approaches often assume homogeneous feature spaces, abundant labeled data, and static distributions. These assumptions rarely hold in real-world predictive settings. Data collected from different sources frequently exhibit variations in semantics, structure, quality, and temporal dynamics. Labels are often scarce, incomplete, or expensive to obtain. Moreover, predictive systems deployed in operational settings must generalize across domains, evolving environments, and previously unseen data distributions. This dissertation investigates predictive modeling under heterogeneous data conditions through a collection of studies spanning social media analytics, environmental hazard prediction, graph representation learning, and scientific knowledge extraction. Although these applications originate from different domains, they share a common objective: transforming fragmented and structurally diverse data into meaningful predictive representations that support inference and decision-making. The first component of this work focuses on predictive modeling in social media environments. Online platforms contain large volumes of user-generated content that can support the analysis of public discourse, user engagement, and community behavior. However, differences in platform characteristics and annotation availability complicate cross-platform prediction tasks. One study addresses this challenge through a transfer learning framework that predicts topic relevance in Reddit using annotated Twitter data and weak supervision derived from Wikipedia. By incorporating domain-adversarial adaptation, the framework improves generalization across heterogeneous social media platforms. A second study models Reddit user interaction and experience using heterogeneous graph representations that integrate user behavior, subreddit relationships, and semantic textual embeddings. These approaches demonstrate the importance of representation learning and relational modeling for predictive analysis in socially generated data. The second component addresses predictive modeling for environmental hazards, with a particular emphasis on landslide susceptibility prediction. Environmental prediction problems require the integration of multimodal geospatial and temporal information derived from weather systems, vegetation patterns, topographical characteristics, and soil conditions. One study develops a machine learning framework that combines heterogeneous environmental variables to estimate landslide susceptibility while addressing challenges associated with class imbalance and high-dimensional data. A subsequent study extends this framework by incorporating Physics-Informed Neural Networks to model soil moisture dynamics and rainfall-induced landslide behavior. By integrating physical constraints with data-driven learning, this work demonstrates how domain knowledge can improve predictive reliability in complex environmental systems. The dissertation also includes two ongoing projects that further extend predictive modeling capabilities for heterogeneous data environments. The first introduces TML-Mixer, a framework for temporal multilayer graph representation learning that captures evolving dependencies across interconnected graph layers. This work addresses the growing need for predictive models capable of representing dynamic relational systems over time. The second project focuses on scientific knowledge extraction through the development of a containerized large language model framework for identifying publications containing phylogenetic tree representations. This work explores the use of large language models and metadata-driven classification for scalable scientific data curation. Collectively, these studies contribute to a broader research agenda centered on predictive modeling with heterogeneous data sources. Across domains, the dissertation investigates how machine learning models can integrate multimodal information, learn robust representations, adapt across distributions, and incorporate structural or scientific knowledge to improve predictive performance in complex real-world environments.

title: PlanarCityLoc: Breaking Silhouette Ambiguity in LoD Aerial Localization via 3D Planes
abstract: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. Experiments on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2 achieve state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods. By grounding image-space alignment in 3D planes, PlanarCityLoc enables more accurate aerial localization with lightweight, textureless city maps.

title: Enhancing trustworthiness in federated learning for disease prediction
abstract: Trustworthy disease prediction in distributed biomedical settings requires more than high predictive accuracy. In practice, collaborative machine learning systems must also protect sensitive patient data, reduce harmful bias across demographic groups, remain feasible under communication and computational constraints, and continue to perform well when data distributions differ across institutions. This dissertation studies these challenges through the lens of federated and collaborative learning and develops methods that improve trustworthiness across four connected dimensions: privacy, fairness, efficiency, and robustness under heterogeneity. The first contribution is FedDP, a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for disease prediction on imbalanced biomedical data. FedDP integrates differential privacy (DP) into collaborative training and combines it with an AUC-oriented min--max optimization strategy to reduce the performance degradation that often occurs under severe label imbalance. The second contribution is MDANN, a fairness-aware framework that mitigates bias from multiple sensitive attributes by combining representation learning, adversarial debiasing, and imbalance-aware optimization. The third contribution is FSLearning, a hybrid framework that combines federated learning and split learning to reduce communication burden in privacy-preserving biomedical imaging analysis through tensor regression. The fourth contribution is FLoRAPID, a parameter-efficient federated learning framework that uses Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and FedMeta-style aggregation to improve communication efficiency and robustness under non-IID client distributions. Across the dissertation, the findings suggest that trustworthiness in distributed disease prediction is not a single property but the outcome of several interacting design choices in optimization, representation learning, aggregation, and system architecture. Overall, this dissertation contributes a set of methods and a broader perspective on how federated and collaborative learning can be made more reliable and practical for biomedical disease prediction. It argues that privacy protection, fairness, efficiency, and robustness should be treated as central design requirements rather than secondary evaluation criteria, and it provides empirical evidence that meaningful progress across these dimensions is possible in real biomedical learning tasks.

title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests
abstract: Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with a separate ensemble of treatment trees. The prior on the leaf values of the treatment trees determines whether sampling variability is attributed to the treatment effect. Independent shrinkage priors exert no control over how a tree allocates variability across its leaves, and their total prior variance grows as leaves are added. We propose the Dirichlet-Tree Bayesian Causal Forest, which jointly regularizes the leaf values of each treatment tree through a Dirichlet-Tree prior on their variance shares, generated by stick-breaking along the tree topology. We characterize the spike and tails of the marginal leaf prior, show that the prior adaptively bounds the number of regions of effect heterogeneity, and establish posterior consistency for the forest. In simulations, the model outperforms BCF when heterogeneity is confined to a few regions and reduces spurious heterogeneity elsewhere, and, unlike independent shrinkage priors, its accuracy does not deteriorate as the trees grow. We also evaluate the model on real data, including a pancreatic cancer survival study.

title: DETECTION OF BITCOIN FRAUD USING VARIATIONAL AUTO ENCODER AND LIGHT GRADIENT BOOSTING MACHINE
abstract: The proliferation of fraudulent behaviour in cryptocurrency ecosystems poses a significant threat to financial security infrastructure. This study develops an approach that uses Variational Autoencoders in combination with Light Gradient Boosting Machines for detecting fraudulent Bitcoin transactions. The Variational Autoencoder component encodes each transaction into a compact latent representation, which is concatenated with the original transaction features to enrich the representation available to the classifier. The Light Gradient Boosting Machine is responsible for classification. Experimental validation on the Elliptic dataset of bitcoin transactions shows the model achieves 99.2% accuracy and 96% F1 score for minority-class detection, outperforming other methods such as Random Forest (95.9% F1), ANN-based models (89.8% F1), and ensemble stacking (97% F1). These results far exceed those of previous approaches, demonstrating the model’s ability to enhance the security and integrity of cryptocurrency transactions.

title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.

title: AI-enabled autonomous knowledge extraction from large-scale textual data
abstract: The rapid growth of large-scale textual data across social media platforms, news media, and scientific repositories presents both unprecedented opportunities and significant challenges for extracting meaningful insights. During global events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, understanding public discourse requires analyzing vast amounts of noisy, heterogeneous, dynamic, and geographically distributed data. At the same time, the exponential increase in scientific publications has made traditional evidence synthesis methods increasingly labor-intensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Existing approaches to textual knowledge extraction often operate in isolation, lack interpretability, fail to integrate heterogeneous data sources, and do not support scalable end-to-end automation. This dissertation addresses these limitations by proposing a unified framework for AI-enabled autonomous knowledge extraction from large-scale textual data. The research introduces a comprehensive pipeline that integrate sentiment analysis, topic modeling, semantic interpretation, spatiotemporal reasoning, and multi-agent automation for scalable, robust and reproducible text analysis across heterogeneous domains. First, this work introduces TriLex, a novel unsupervised sentiment analysis framework that combines multiple lexicon-based sentiment analysis methods through weighted aggregation, majority voting, and dynamic thresholding technique to improve robustness and accuracy for short and noisy textual data. Building on this foundation, a hierarchical spatiotemporal framework is developed to capture the evolution of public sentiment across global, national, and regional scales. The framework integrates over 7 million social media posts and thousands of news articles to analyze COVID-19 vaccine discourse across time, geographic regions, and platforms. To enhance topic interpretability, this research integrates BERTopic with large language models (LLMs), enabling automated generation of coherent and context-aware topic representations for large-scale textual discourse. A cross-platform analytical framework is further introduced to examine temporal relationships between social media and news media discourse, demonstrating a bidirectional relationship in which news coverage and public discourse influence each other over time. Extending beyond discourse analysis, this dissertation introduces an Agentic AI framework that automates the end-to-end process of large-scale multilingual knowledge extraction and evidence synthesis. The proposed multi-agent system coordinates specialized agents for query generation, multilingual retrieval, metadata harmonization, title and abstract screening, and full-text analysis. Evaluated on a multilingual corpus of over 52,000 scientific records, the framework achieves high screening performance while substantially reducing processing time from months to hours, demonstrating significant improvements in scalability, robustness, and reproducibility. Collectively, this dissertation bridges the gap between analytical understanding and autonomous knowledge extraction from large-scale textual data. By integrating robust sentiment analysis, interpretable topic modeling, spatiotemporal discourse analysis, and autonomous AI systems within a unified framework, this work establishes a scalable and extensible paradigm for transforming heterogeneous textual data into actionable knowledge. The proposed methodologies are validated using real-world datasets spanning social media, news media, and scientific literature across diverse application domains.

title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

title: A Flexible ROI Analysis Tool for Spatially Consistent Vegetation Index Extraction from Turfgrass Imagery
abstract: Time-series multispectral imaging is widely used to assess turfgrass condition; however, extracting plot-level vegetation index (VI) values remains labor-intensive when camera positions vary between acquisitions and automated plot tracking is unreliable. We developed an open-source software tool comprising (i) a graphical user interface (GUI) for the interactive placement of orientation-adjustable regions of interest (ROIs) with $N$-way subdivision to match plot geometry and (ii) a batch-processing script that computes plot-level mean VI values from single-band floating-point rasters and exports measurements and ROI coordinates in JSON format for reuse. Saved coordinates can be reapplied to measure NDVI, NDRE, and SAVI from identical pixel regions within a single time point without re-delineating ROIs. In a demonstration using rail-mounted multispectral turfgrass imagery (18 images), plot-level mean values were extracted in a single session, with coordinates reused directly for NDRE and SAVI rasters. The system reads non-georeferenced pixel-coordinate rasters natively, does not require GIS expertise, and supports reproducible VI quantification where static sensor deployment is impractical.

title: LLM-assisted relevance screening of EU research projects for the TRIMIS transport database – validation outputs and analysis code
abstract: This dataset contains the outputs used to evaluate how well large language models (LLMs) can identify transport-relevant research projects for TRIMIS, the European Commission's Transport Research and Innovation Monitoring and Information System. A random sample of 250 Horizon Europe projects from CORDIS was labelled by domain experts as not relevant, partly relevant or relevant to transport. The same projects were then scored by four open-weight LLMs, each run with 13 different prompts, giving 52 sets of results. Each file lists, per project, the expert label, the model's score, its justification and supporting quotation, and processing cost. The package also includes the prompts, a Python script that recomputes all reported statistics, and the resulting tables and charts. It supports the article "Enhancing Transport Innovation Knowledge Management Workflows Using Artificial Intelligence: A TRIMIS Database Case Study" (European Transport Research Review, 2026).

title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

title: HoloCosm: Beyond Single-Metric Benchmark Compression Across Multiple Metrics
abstract: Benchmark compression reduces evaluation cost by selecting a small set of samples. Existing methods typically guide selection using a single metric, although benchmarks often assess models along multiple dimensions. We find that model rankings are often weakly correlated across metrics, indicating that different metrics capture distinct aspects of model performance. Samples selected for one metric do not reliably preserve scores and rankings on others when used for compressed evaluation. At 80\% compression, each of the five single-metric baselines yields higher reconstruction error than equal-size random sampling in over 70\% of cross-metric comparisons. To address this challenge, we present HoloCosm, which jointly minimizes normalized score-reconstruction error across source models and metrics while constraining ranking distortion. We evaluate HoloCosm across multiple compression rates on 15 language, multimodal, VLA, and agent benchmark configurations with 85 component metrics. With 80\% compression, HoloCosm outperforms Random, the strongest baseline overall: average NMAE drops by 35.3\% to 0.236, worst-component NMAE drops by 39.5\% to 0.330, and average Spearman correlation rises from 0.884 to 0.915. In addition, HoloCosm remains competitive with existing baselines in single-metric evaluation. We will release our code and experimental results.

title: A LIGHTWEIGHT CUSTOM CNN FOR ROBUST AND CLINICALLY SAFE CT KIDNEY DISEASE CLASSIFICATION
abstract: ABSTRACT: Kidney diseases such as renal cysts, stone, and malignant tumors represent a significant and increasing health burden worldwide. Manual CT diagnosis is labour-intensive and has high inter-observer variability, which requires the support of automatic diagnosis. In this paper, a lightweighted custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is proposed, which is used to automatically classify kidney computed tomography (CT) images into four classes: Cyst, Normal, Stone, and Tumor. It includes residual skip connections, a dual-pooling head (Global Average and Global Max Pooling), Spatial Dropout2D regularization, and a composite training objective that explicitly favors Tumor Recall. The CT-KIDNEY-DATASET was mad leakage-safe through MD5 exact deduplication and perceptual-hash grouping, so that all reported evaluations are free of data leakage. Across the five validation folds, KidneyCNN achieved a mean accuracy of 99.82 ± 0.06% and a mean Tumor Recall of 99.31 ± 0.30%. Separately, ensemble inference on the independent held-out test set of 1,904 images achieved 99.84% accuracy, with AUC = 1.000 for all classes and only three misclassifications. The Grad-CAM++ results show that the model attention as anatomically relevant, which further indicates that KidneyCNN is a clinically safe and deployable kidney disease screening tool.

title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

title: From utterances to actionable labels: Toward practical and scalable open intent discovery in production systems
abstract: This thesis presents novel contributions to the field of Open Intent Discovery (OID), addressing fundamental challenges in the unsupervised identification and labelling of user intents within unlabelled datasets. Existing work in OID often relies on small, static, and clean datasets, lacks robust methods for generating interpretable intent labels, and exhibits inconsistencies in evaluation methodologies. This research responds to these gaps by introducing a modular, fully unsupervised framework that supports the complete OID pipeline, from clustering to label generation, without requiring labelled data or large-scale pre-trained language models. A key academic contribution is the development of a fine-grained intent labelling technique based on an enhanced Action-Object extraction method. This method incorporates compound noun and adjective structures to improve the expressiveness and semantic precision of generated labels. The framework enables systematic comparison across different OID configurations, revealing how dataset properties such as utterance length, vocabulary diversity, and intent structure influence algorithm performance. Furthermore, a configuration prediction module is introduced to explore the feasibility of automating technique selection based on dataset features. It also exposes limitations in current evaluation strategies for label quality, underscoring the need for more nuanced, semantically grounded metrics. Collectively, the findings advance the theoretical understanding of unsupervised intent discovery and lay the foundation for future research in label generation, evaluation, and adaptive configuration in the broader field of natural language understanding.

title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
abstract: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.

title: A novel semi-supervised few-shot learning framework for Arabic text sentiment classification in low-resource settings.
abstract: The proliferation of user-generated content on social media platforms offers vast potential for sentiment analysis, enabling real-time insights into public opinions and social trends. However, effective sentiment detection from short Arabic texts remains a challenge due to the availability of limited annotated data, the complex morphology of Arabic and dialectal diversity. Despite significant advances in natural language understanding for languages such as English, Arabic remains a low-resource language and is often underserved by recent state-of-the-art solutions. To address these challenges, this thesis presents several original contributions. We first addressed data scarcity in the tourism domain—a sector with limited research in Arabic—by creating a corpus of 2,293 Arabic tweets, automatically annotated with sentiment labels using a zero-shot Transformer-based method and benchmarked against manually labelled annotations. Building on this dataset generation, we proposed a novel few-shot learning method for Arabic text classification, which is composed of two main phases. In the first phase, we employed a multifeature fusion approach, utilizing hybrid semi-supervised Arabic BERT-based large language models. These features were further enhanced by incorporating class labels’ semantics as auxiliary features to assist in capturing contextual information within short texts. Afterwards, in the second phase we utilized a prototypical network relying on episodic learning to generate prototype vectors calculated for each class by calculating the mean of embedding features of the support text inputs that correspond to that class. Classification is conducted after generating these prototypes by using a similarity distance-based non-parametric classifier and a softmax function over the distances between all class prototype vectors and the target query text input vector. Our model was rigorously evaluated on multiple benchmark Arabic datasets and on our generated dataset which supported our framework’s adaptability and validated its robustness. Thus, experimental results demonstrated that our proposed method surpasses typical few-shot learning methods and significantly improved performance in domains with scarce data. We also contributed to alleviate the problem of Arabic as a low-resource language by designing a zero-shot cross-domain classification method by developing a generalized TRUE/FALSE decoder instead of the traditional task-specific decoder and a fine-tuned model encoder sharing the entire model across different tasks. This method exquisitely detected Arabic sarcasm utilizing a sentiment-trained model and vice versa. Additionally, we examined the generated few-shot meta-learner scalability to bilingual datasets (English and Arabic) by leveraging language models designed for few-shot learning utilizing hypernetwork-based task adaptation across diverse language domains.

title: HandsOn: A Large-Scale Simulation Benchmark for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes. The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations. Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer. Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success. Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks. HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.

title: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge
abstract: A key problem in AI safety is eliciting latent knowledge (ELK), extracting information from a model that is misaligned and more knowledgeable than its overseer. For example, a misaligned model used to scan code for vulnerabilities may want to withhold its findings, i.e., sandbag, in order to exploit them later. To study ELK empirically, we need model organisms that mirror this setting. Existing model organisms fall short in several respects. In this work, we train model organisms to withhold solutions in a vulnerability detection task. We combine transcript distillation with counter-prompting and tamper-resistance training to instill three properties that we argue are critical for a useful ELK testbed: 1) Selectivity, the model sandbags when it thinks the overseer doesn't know the answer and complies otherwise, 2) Robustness, the model resists elicitation, and 3) Retention, the model retains a knowledge advantage over the overseer, as opposed to losing the relevant capability. We train a sequence of model organisms and show that our strongest model substantially outperforms prior models on robustness while keeping the other two properties intact. We hope that our model organisms provide a useful ELK testbed for the community, and that our methodology sparks the development of increasingly challenging model organisms. All our code, models and the dataset are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/lennart-finke/sandbagging.

title: Towards an explainable Arabic sentiment analysis framework
abstract: Individuals frequently express emotions and opinions through online social platforms such as Twitter, now rebranded as X. Recognizing and accurately interpreting sentiments in social media content provides substantial benefits to sectors such as government, healthcare, social services, business, and market research. Although deep neural network-based models have achieved high performance in sentiment analysis tasks, their inherent lack of interpretability raises significant concerns about transparency, reliability, and trustworthiness. This thesis presents distinct complementary contributions to address these interpretability challenges. Initially, it offers a comprehensive, pioneering survey that systematically examines prominent sentiment analysis techniques within the scope of eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Following this, the thesis introduces novel methodological advancements, notably an automated annotation method specifically developed for the Twitter-based Arabic Mental Illness (AMI) dataset. This approach leverages existing manually annotated datasets and applies transfer learning using three advanced Arabic pre-trained language models, effectively streamlining annotation processes and enriching the Arabic language resources available for sentiment analysis. To achieve robust explainability, a two-fold interpretability framework is proposed. The first component utilizes dependency-based rules and specific linguistic patterns, including syntactic dependencies and word polarity relationships, enabling accurate sentiment identification by analysing dependent word structures within sentences. The second component employs knowledge distillation, transferring insights from complex deep neural networks to simpler, inherently interpretable models, thus ensuring global interpretability. Three distinct knowledge distillation pipelines are investigated to effectively transfer knowledge from sophisticated neural architectures into transparent, interpretable models. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on the AMI Arabic sentiment analysis dataset demonstrate that the proposed methodologies consistently outperform traditional baseline models. Additionally, the thesis scales the knowledge distillation approach to multilingual sentiment analysis encompassing both Arabic and English. Importantly, it demonstrates that the core knowledge distillation methodology remains consistently effective across languages without requiring language-specific modifications. By integrating Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) with knowledge distillation, the thesis significantly enhances the interpretability of multilingual large language models at both local and global levels, promoting improved model reliability and practical deployment in diverse multilingual environments.

title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.

title: RAG Hallucination Benchmark for Teaching Knowledge Bases
authors: Atlanta College of Liberal Arts and Sciences
abstract: How often does a small RAG system invent answers when the knowledge base does not contain them? This benchmark measures hallucination rates of a 0.5B model (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct) on 30 teaching-domain questions (10 answerable / 10 partial / 10 unanswerable) across 3 RAG configurations. Key finding: 30-70% hallucination rate despite explicit grounding instructions; increasing top_k from 3 to 5 halved hallucinations. Part of Study Intelligence, the open research program of the Atlanta College of Liberal Arts and Sciences (ACLAS).

title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm.

title: Foundation Model Driven Optical Flow
abstract: We investigate how frozen pretrained visual and depth representations support dense optical flow when coupled with a supervised matching network. Building on TTSFlow, this paper studies Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) feature decoding and one coarse-to-fine refinement stage. Our method fuses features from frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 models and estimates optical flow through a trainable transformer-based matching pipeline. After optical-flow training on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D, it achieves 2.37 endpoint error (EPE) on the Sintel training split, Final pass, compared with 2.52 for the FlowSeek (T) configuration reported here. Our RoCo-Spring 2026 entry, RoCo-29.VSAI, obtains a robustness-balanced score of 1.1038, Spring EPE of 1.411, and RobustSpring proxy EPE of 4.739, with a lower balanced score than seven of the twelve listed reference baselines. These results characterize the complete pipeline, which reuses frozen foundation backbones and performs one refinement stage. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/Visual-and-Spatial-AI-Lab/FFlow}

title: PatchCraft: image patch extraction, reconstruction, pairing and seam-aware stitching
abstract: PatchCraft cuts one image into patches and puts it back. One call takes one (C, H, W) float tensor and returns one tensor: there is no batch axis, no dataset, no dataloader and no model, and that boundary is documented as binding rather than provisional. It owns the unfold and fold arithmetic, the geometry validation and the seam blending, so a pipeline can own the rest. Two silent defects motivate it. The intuitive reshape of F.unfold's output gives the right shape with the wrong pixels, and a stride that does not cover the image leaves pixels at zero without any error: on a 128 by 128 image with patch 32 and stride 20, 3840 of 16384 pixels. Both are checked once here, with tests around them. The numeric contract is stated as a caller-evaluable predicate rather than a promise. The extract and reconstruct round trip is bit-exact if and only if every value of the overlap coverage map is a power of two, always true at stride equal to patch size, and outside that rule the per-pixel error is bounded by (k+1) times eps times the absolute value, with k the pixel's coverage count. A falsification suite enumerates the 126,736 legal geometries of the space independently of the predicate and tries to break both halves of it. Five of the six published wheels carry a Rust kernel for the overlapping fold, compiled into the wheel itself rather than into a separate package, and bit-identical to the pure-torch path by test. Every other platform installs a universal wheel and runs the same operation in torch. Pre-1.0: output values may change when the middle digit moves, and the changelog records each change with the measurement behind it.

title: Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: Mitigating Rubric Hacking through Latent Dimension Recovery and Balancing
abstract: Rubric hacking limits both performance and training robustness in rubric-based reinforcement learning. By decomposing rubrics into sub-dimensions, we reveal the Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: as the total rubric score increases, certain sub-dimension scores systematically decrease, suggesting the model sacrifices specific quality aspects to optimize the aggregated objective. From the sub-dimension perspective, we observe two phenomena: (1) dimension imbalance, causing the policy to favor heavily covered dimensions; (2) dimension absence, leading to a systematic gap between rewards and true quality. To mitigate these issues, we propose Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA), which has generations compete within each dimension separately to mitigate rubric imbalance, and Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC), which mines evaluation dimensions implicitly encoded in a holistic preference signal to complete rubric coverage. Experiments in chat, science, and medical domains indicate that FRDA mitigates rubric hacking with more stable improvements, while RSDC outperforms both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation, yielding generally higher-quality responses.

title: Post-Quantum Oblivious Transfer for Oblivious Inference on Resource-Constrained Devices
abstract: Oblivious inference (OI) systems such as MiniONN, GAZELLE and DELPHI rely on oblivious transfer (OT) bootstrapped from base OTs whose security rests on CDH or DDH, which Shor’s algorithm breaks; for longlived IIoT deployments, Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later makes this a current concern. We review post-quantum (PQ) OT protocols published 2008–2026 against five axes: UC security, adversarial model, security model (ROM, QROM, CRS, standard model), round complexity, and reported benchmarks. Within our corpus, only lattice-based OT has measured performance on ARM application-class cores: ROTed reports 191 µs (286.5 k cycles) per ROT on a Cortex-A72, excluding network latency and randomness generation. Isogeny-based OT has the smallest messages but no reported implementation. We find two gaps: no implemented PQ base OT that UC-realises standard or random OT has a QROM proof, while the RO-free UC constructions are unimplemented; and no PQ base OT has been measured on microcontroller-class hardware.

title: BrushOff: Stroke-Based Re-rendering as a Watermark Removal Attack on Painting
abstract: Invisible watermarks are used to mark who owns a painting. We show that a simple attack removes the most robust one we test. The attack redraws the watermarked painting with brush strokes, using a pretrained stroke-based renderer. We call this attack BrushOff. It needs no training, no knowledge of the watermark, and no generative model. We test four watermarks on 500 paintings from five styles. VINE, a recent watermark built to survive image editing, survives all 14 conventional distortions we test, with at least 97.8% detection. Repainting lowers its detection to 1.8%, while the output keeps a no-reference quality score close to that of the clean paintings. Diffusion regeneration can also remove VINE, but at the same removal level it moves the image twice as far from the painting in DreamSim distance, and it changes what the painting shows. Because the renderer draws a countable number of strokes, we can control the attack strength step by step. Finally, we test what kind of signal survives. A simple probe that stores bits in the relative brightness of neighboring regions survives repainting, while a probe that uses absolute brightness does not. The same probe fails under diffusion regeneration, while VINE fails under repainting. Robustness to these two attacks is therefore a separate property, and benchmarks should test both.

title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models
abstract: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.

title: Real-Time Classification of Low Probability of Intercept Signals Using an End-to-End Neural Network (EELPINet)
abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end neural network for real-time classification of low probability of intercept (LPI) radar signals using raw complex-valued inputs. Conventional LPI signal classification methods typically rely on time–frequency preprocessing, such as short-time Fourier transform or Wigner–Ville distribution, which introduces additional computational overhead and may distort signal characteristics under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. To address these limitations, the proposed method directly processes raw in-phase and quadrature signal sequences without explicit time–frequency analysis. The proposed network consists of a lightweight raw signal feature extractor and a sequence analysis module based on a state-space model, enabling efficient modeling of long-range temporal dependencies. In addition, a Gaussian-based padding strategy is employed to handle variable-length input signals while preserving statistical continuity. Experimental evaluations were conducted using a large-scale simulated LPI radar dataset covering multiple modulation types and SNR levels ranging from –16 dB to 10 dB. The proposed method achieved an average classification accuracy of 90.99% with low computational complexity, requiring only 1.62 GFLOPs and 3.73 ms inference time per sample. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective and suitable for real-time LPI radar signal classification in electronic warfare environments.

title: AI-Assisted Sentiment Analysis of Student Voice: A Human-Validated Comparison of Lexicon and Transformer-Based Tools
abstract: Open-ended survey responses offer rich insights into the student experience, yet analyzing this qualitative data at scale is often time-consuming and labor-intensive. This study evaluates whether off-the-shelf sentiment analysis tools can validly classify such data for institutional assessment. Analyzing 1,220 free-text responses from undergraduate students at a private liberal arts university, we compared the performance of four tools: two lexicon-based (TextBlob and VADER) and two transformer-based (BERT-nlptown and RoBERTa-cardiffnlp) against manual coding. Evaluation metrics included accuracy, macro F1 score, and Cohen’s kappa (κ). While BERT-nlptown performed best, it achieved only moderate agreement with human coding (κ = .42). Furthermore, lexicon-based approaches misclassified roughly 20% of responses due to limited vocabulary coverage. Notably, all tools struggled to accurately classify negative, neutral and mixed sentiments. We recommend conducting lexicon-coverage diagnostics, few-shot prompting, domain-specific finetuning, and human-in-the-loop oversight to ensure valid, reliable, and trustworthy institutional assessment.

title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents
abstract: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.

title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
abstract: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

title: PrismWAM: Decoupling State Representations in World Action Models
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically represent the world through latent embeddings from pretrained video models, which entangle heterogeneous aspects of the world, from how it looks (e.g., texture and color) to how it is physically configured (e.g., occupancy and pose). This raises an underexplored question: what should constitute the state of a WAM? We argue that the world state should separate how the world appears from how the world evolves under action: the former captures semantic context, while the latter is governed by physical state. To this end, we propose PrismWAM, which decouples physics from semantics while jointly modeling state and action. PrismWAM factorizes an embodied task into a Semantic PlanningrightarrowPhysical RolloutrightarrowExecutable Action pipeline: given only the initial RGB observation, semantic planning learns to predict the final goal image, while physical rollout predicts the fine-grained evolution toward this goal in depth space; executable actions are then generated from the depth rollout. Without any embodied action pretraining or additional data augmentation, PrismWAM achieves strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world. Notably, PrismWAM even surpasses a broad range of models with large-scale embodied action pretraining (e.g., OpenWAM-α). More broadly, we reframe World Action Models from modeling how the world looks to how it responds to action, paving the way for action-centric world models grounded in occupancy, flow, tactile sensing, proprioception, and beyond.

title: Reproducibility Package for "Multi-Representation Stylometry of Al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya: Internal Consistency and Register Variation in Classical Arabic"
abstract: This reproducibility package accompanies the manuscript “Multi-Representation Stylometry of Al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya: Internal Consistency and Register Variation in Classical Arabic.” It includes the corpus metadata and frozen hashes, the Gold-V3 segmentation benchmark, segmenter validation records, normalized feature matrices, PCA materials, Eder results, robustness results, reproduction code, software and environment information, checksums, provenance records, and the publication figures. The complete transformed text of the modern edition and the full ArabicSOS production output are not included because their redistribution rights are still unresolved. Their frozen SHA-256 identifiers are provided instead. The main Eder hierarchical-clustering analyses and the matched-length Eder results can be reproduced from the matrices and code included in the package.
